course.title: Data Visualization with Python (matplotlib)
course.description: Turn data into charts in your browser with matplotlib — line plots, bar charts, and scatter plots — writing real Python whose output you see rendered instantly, with the underlying data auto-checked. Structure informed by the open Matplotlib documentation (BSD-style license).

questions.prompt: In matplotlib, which function draws a line connecting a series of points?
questions.explanation: plt.plot(x, y) draws a line (and/or markers) through the points; plt.bar and plt.scatter draw bars and points.

questions.prompt: Which chart is best for comparing a value across a few named categories?
questions.explanation: A bar chart compares a measure across discrete categories; lines suit trends over an ordered axis.

questions.prompt: Which chart best shows the relationship between two numeric variables?
questions.explanation: A scatter plot places each observation as a point (x, y), revealing correlation and clusters.

questions.prompt: How do you add a title to the current matplotlib figure?
questions.explanation: plt.title('...') sets the title; plt.xlabel/ylabel label the axes.

questions.prompt: What is the conventional import for matplotlib's plotting interface?
options: from matplotlib import chart as plt
questions.explanation: The near-universal convention is import matplotlib.pyplot as plt.

questions.prompt: A dict {'a': 2, 'b': 1} counting how often each item appears is often shown as a…
questions.explanation: Category counts map naturally to a bar chart: one bar per key, height = count.

lessons.title: Plotting with matplotlib
lessons.grammar_note: Build a chart by calling plotting functions in order: first the data (plt.plot / plt.bar / plt.scatter), then labels (plt.title, plt.xlabel, plt.ylabel). Each call adds to the current figure.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Draw line, bar, and scatter charts with matplotlib and label them clearly. Warm-up: which function would you use to connect points into a trend line?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: matplotlib's pyplot interface (imported as plt) draws into a current figure. plt.plot(x, y) draws a line through the points; add marker='o' to show the points too. plt.bar(labels, heights) draws one bar per label. plt.scatter(x, y) places a dot for each pair. Label everything: plt.title('...'), plt.xlabel('...'), plt.ylabel('...'). In these lessons the chart is drawn for you from your function's output — your job is to return the right data, and you'll see it rendered.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: A line of squares: plt.plot([0,1,2,3], [0,1,4,9], marker='o'); plt.title('Squares'). A bar chart of counts: plt.bar(['a','b','c'], [3,1,2]); plt.ylabel('count'). A scatter of two variables: plt.scatter([1,2,3,4], [2,4,5,4]); plt.xlabel('x'); plt.ylabel('y'). Each of these adds marks to the current figure, which is then displayed.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Match the chart to the task. 1) Sales each month over a year. 2) Number of users per country (5 countries). 3) Height vs. weight for 100 people. 4) A single running total climbing over time. Answers: 1) line. 2) bar. 3) scatter. 4) line.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: using a line chart for unordered categories — bars are clearer. Mistake: forgetting axis labels, so the reader cannot tell what the numbers mean. Exit: (a) Which function draws bars? (b) Which draws a point per (x, y) pair? Answers: plt.bar; plt.scatter.

body.prompt: Write first_squares(n) that returns the first n square numbers as a plain list: [0, 1, 4, 9, ...] (that is, i*i for i from 0 to n-1). Use numpy. The starter draws your result as a line chart.
body.instructions: Fill in the function; the code below it already plots what you return, so you'll see the line appear. Tests check the returned list. First run downloads the runtime + libraries once.
body.starter:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

def first_squares(n):
    # return the first n squares as a plain list, using numpy
    return []

# Draw the result (runs when you click Run):
ys = first_squares(10)
plt.plot(range(len(ys)), ys, marker="o")
plt.title("First squares")
plt.xlabel("i"); plt.ylabel("i squared")
body.solution:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

def first_squares(n):
    return (np.arange(n) ** 2).tolist()

ys = first_squares(10)
plt.plot(range(len(ys)), ys, marker="o")
plt.title("First squares")
plt.xlabel("i"); plt.ylabel("i squared")

lessons.title: Bar charts and scatter plots
lessons.grammar_note: A Python dict is the natural home for category -> value data. dict.get(key, 0) returns 0 when a key is missing — handy for counting without a KeyError.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Count categories into a dict and show them as a bar chart, and plot two numeric variables as a scatter. Warm-up: what does {}.get('x', 0) return?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: To count how often each value appears, walk the list and increment a dict: counts[item] = counts.get(item, 0) + 1. The result, e.g. {'apple': 3, 'banana': 2}, maps directly onto a bar chart: plt.bar(list(counts.keys()), list(counts.values())). For two numeric variables, a scatter plot shows each observation as a point: plt.scatter(xs, ys). Scatters reveal whether y tends to rise with x (positive relationship), fall (negative), or neither.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Counting: for it in ['a','b','a']: counts[it] = counts.get(it, 0) + 1 yields {'a': 2, 'b': 1}. Plot it: plt.bar(list(counts.keys()), list(counts.values())). Scatter: plt.scatter([1,2,3,4], [2,3,5,4]); plt.xlabel('x'); plt.ylabel('y') places four points. If you also compute a summary like the average, you can annotate it, but the scatter alone already shows the shape of the data.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) After counting ['x','y','x','x'], what is the dict? 2) Which chart shows counts per category? 3) Which chart shows height vs. weight? 4) What does {'a':1}.get('b', 0) return? Answers: 1) {'x': 3, 'y': 1}. 2) bar. 3) scatter. 4) 0.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: indexing a missing dict key (counts[item] += 1 on the first sighting) raises KeyError — use .get(item, 0). Mistake: passing dict_keys directly where a list is expected; wrap with list(). Exit: (a) How do you count into a dict safely? (b) Which chart pairs two numeric variables? Answers: counts.get(k, 0) + 1; scatter.

lessons.title: Code: a bar chart of counts

body.prompt: Write category_counts(items) that returns a dict mapping each string in the list `items` to how many times it appears. The starter draws the counts as a bar chart.
body.instructions: Count each item into a dict (hint: use counts.get(item, 0) + 1). The code below plots whatever you return. Tests check the dict.
body.starter:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

def category_counts(items):
    counts = {}
    # count each item into counts
    return counts

data = ["apple", "banana", "apple", "cherry", "banana", "apple"]
counts = category_counts(data)
plt.bar(list(counts.keys()), list(counts.values()))
plt.title("Fruit counts"); plt.ylabel("count")

questions.explanation: plt.plot connects the (x, y) points with a line (and optional markers).

questions.prompt: To count occurrences into a dict without a KeyError, use…
questions.explanation: counts.get(item, 0) returns 0 for a new key, so the increment is safe.

questions.prompt: Which chart best compares a value across named categories?
questions.explanation: Bars make category comparisons easy to read.

options: show each (x, y) as a point
questions.explanation: A scatter plot draws one dot per observation, showing the relationship between x and y.
keys() gives the dict's keys; list() turns them into ['a', 'b'].

questions.prompt: Which sets the label on the y-axis?
questions.explanation: plt.ylabel('...') labels the vertical axis; plt.xlabel labels the horizontal one.
